items: Schedule a vet appointment this week for sudden behavior changes — sudden aggression, inappropriate elimination, nighttime vocalization, and destructiveness have a medical root cause in the majority of documented cases and need diagnosis before behavioral training begins.

Request a urinalysis to check for UTI, crystals, and bladder cells — urinary issues cause cats to avoid the litter box because they associate it with pain, and this test identifies the most common medical cause of inappropriate urination.

Request a senior blood panel checking kidney function, thyroid levels, and blood sugar — these two tests catch the majority of medical causes for behavioral change and typically cost between $150–$350 depending on your area.

Write down all recent behavior changes before your vet visit — list aggression, nighttime vocalization, litter box issues, and destructiveness with when each started so your vet has complete information for diagnosis.

Schedule two 10-minute wand toy play sessions per day — one in the morning before work and one in the evening after dinner — because cats who complete the hunt cycle 2–3 times daily are calmer and less destructive.
Move wand toys erratically with short dashes, sudden stops, and direction changes — mimicking real prey movement satisfies your cat's stalking instinct before you let them catch the toy.
Let your cat physically catch and "kill" the toy at the end of each session — a cat who stalks and chases but never catches becomes more frustrated, not less, so always end with the capture moment.

Feed 3–5 treats immediately after each play session to complete the Hunt-Catch-Kill-Eat cycle — this mirrors the natural post-hunt meal and creates behavioral satisfaction that bowl feeding cannot provide.

Replace bowl feeding entirely with food puzzles to turn mealtime into a hunt — puzzles provide mental stimulation equivalent to 30–60 minutes of interactive play per day and reduce boredom-based destruction.
Make a toilet paper roll puzzle by rolling both ends closed, poking small holes in it, and filling it with kibble — cats spend 5–10 minutes working it open and this costs nothing to create.
Place kibble in a muffin tin's wells and cover each well with a tennis ball — your cat must nose out each ball to access food, turning breakfast into a challenging hunt activity.
Fill a loosely closed Amazon box with kibble and tear several holes in the sides — scatter the kibble throughout the box so your cat works to retrieve pieces, replicating natural hunting conditions.
